Financial planning · Loss and recovery arithmetic · Visual planning guide

After a portfolio loss, recovering the old balance and recovering purchasing power are different targets

Calculate the gain needed after a loss, distinguish cumulative from annual recovery requirements, and separate new deposits from subsequent investment growth.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate a nominal recovery, purchasing power and new deposits

Original deterministic illustration: an immediate one-time loss is followed by the selected number of whole years of a constant nominal annual total return. Each year’s return applies before that year-end deposit. The original purchasing-power target rises at the selected constant annual inflation rate from the instant after the loss. All distributions remain within total return. No fees, taxes, withdrawals, historical returns, probabilities or future-return forecasts are included. Required gains are arithmetic thresholds, not returns that an investment promises to deliver. Initial loss remains below 100%, so all recovery denominators are positive.

The central idea

A gain applies to the capital that remains. Inflation can move the target, while new saving can restore an account balance without being investment performance.

01

Measure the required gain from the capital that remains

A loss and a later gain use different starting amounts. In this hypothetical example, a CAD 100,000 portfolio loses 30% immediately and falls to CAD 70,000. Regaining CAD 30,000 requires a gain of approximately 42.86% on the remaining CAD 70,000.

Applying a 30% gain instead produces CAD 91,000. The same percentage with the opposite sign does not undo the loss because its denominator is smaller. In general, a fractional loss L requires a subsequent gain of L divided by (1 minus L) to regain the original nominal amount, assuming no deposits or withdrawals.

The loss control stops below 100%. At a total loss, there is no remaining capital on which a percentage recovery can operate. This arithmetic does not identify an investment that will produce the required gain. Investor.gov’s risk explanation emphasizes that invested principal can be lost.

02

A fixed dollar target can lose purchasing power while you wait

The second target preserves what the original capital could buy, using the selected constant price-growth assumption. At 2% annual inflation for ten years, CAD 100,000 of original purchasing power becomes a nominal target of approximately CAD 121,899.44.

Reaching that amount from CAD 70,000 requires a cumulative gain of approximately 74.14% without new deposits. This is larger than the 42.86% required merely to regain the old dollar amount. The first chart displays both cumulative requirements over the selected horizon.

The inflation input is an authored assumption, not a current CPI observation or a forecast of the household’s spending basket. Investor.gov discusses inflation risk as a loss of buying power when money fails to keep pace with prices. The personal-inflation guide can help distinguish a broad price index from a particular household goal.

03

Convert the horizon into an annual requirement carefully

The headline annual requirement is the constant compound rate that would take post-loss capital to the purchasing-power target over the selected whole years, without any new deposits. It equals the target-to-remaining-capital ratio raised to one divided by the number of years, minus one.

In the default, that rate is approximately 5.70% annually. It is not the 74.14% cumulative requirement divided by ten, and it is not an available yield. A required return describes the mathematics of a goal; it does not establish that the risk needed to pursue it is affordable.

Changing the horizon changes both the compounding time and the inflation-adjusted target. A longer interval gives capital more time to grow but also gives prices more time to rise. The calculation keeps those two effects inside the same equation rather than subtracting a rough inflation allowance from a cumulative percentage.

04

Compare the paths using the same year-end checkpoints

The path chart begins immediately after the loss. Both portfolios then receive the selected constant nominal annual total return. One receives no further money. The other receives the selected deposit after each year’s return, so a new contribution first earns a return in the following year.

At 5% for ten years, the no-deposit portfolio ends near CAD 114,022.62. It first regains the old CAD 100,000 amount at the eighth annual checkpoint, but it never reaches the moving purchasing-power target within the modeled ten years.

The chart tests only those whole-year checkpoints. It does not estimate an actual recovery date, a typical market waiting time or the likelihood of another loss. Its smooth return assumption deliberately removes volatility so that the denominator, inflation and deposit effects can be inspected separately.

05

Reconcile new saving before describing performance

With CAD 3,000 deposited at every year-end, the default ending portfolio is approximately CAD 151,756.30. The household added CAD 30,000 after the loss. Subtracting that cash and the CAD 70,000 post-loss starting amount leaves approximately CAD 51,756.30 of subsequent modeled investment growth.

The waterfall uses those three components. It does not subtract the original CAD 30,000 loss again, because that loss is already reflected in the CAD 70,000 opening capital. Nor does it call every dollar above the old statement balance an investment profit.

A deposit can bring an account back above its previous high even when investment performance has not recovered. Keep contribution records beside the statement. This dollar reconciliation is not an annual performance measure, a money-weighted return, a realized capital gain or a determination of tax cost basis.

06

Read the target gap without turning it into a return promise

The matrix varies the immediate loss and subsequent annual return. It keeps the selected capital, horizon, inflation and year-end contributions unchanged. Every cell subtracts the same inflation-adjusted original-capital target from that scenario’s ending portfolio.

A positive amount is a modeled surplus; a negative amount is a modeled shortfall. Neither color reports a probability or says that a portfolio is safe. A household may also need a different target because of withdrawals, changed expenses or an earlier use date. Those changes require their own cash flows rather than an unexplained adjustment to expected returns.

For planning, record three separate facts: capital remaining after the loss, future money that can realistically be added, and the amount and timing of the goal. The model excludes fees and taxes and retains all distributions within total return. Its purpose is to make the recovery arithmetic inspectable before a required percentage is mistaken for a forecast.
